entities.summary:
The 2002–2004 SARS outbreak originated in Foshan, China, on November 16, 2002, and ended on May 19, 2004. The global pandemic caused widespread fear, led to a significant increase in international travel restrictions, and resulted in a substantial economic impact. The outbreak led to the deaths of nearly 774 people and infected over 8,000, with cases reported in 37 countries. The World Health Organization (WHO) played a crucial role in coordinating the global response to the crisis.

The 2002–2004 SARS outbreak was a significant event in modern history, with far-reaching consequences for global health and international relations. The outbreak led to a major overhaul of global health systems, with improved surveillance and response mechanisms put in place. The crisis also highlighted the importance of cooperation and information sharing between countries in the face of a global health threat.

The legacy of the 2002–2004 SARS outbreak can be seen in the way it accelerated the development of global health infrastructure, including the creation of the WHO's Incident Management System. The crisis also led to increased investment in public health research and development of new technologies to combat infectious diseases.

In the words of Dr. Lee Chin-chuan, a Taiwanese virologist who helped identify the SARS virus, 'The SARS outbreak has taught us the importance of global coordination and cooperation in the face of a global health threat.'
